story: Georges Gilles de la Tourette described nine patients in 1885 whose tics came with involuntary sounds. He was later shot in the head by a former patient who believed he had hypnotised her, and survived.

Pasteur was asked why French wine kept going sour. He found living organisms in it and showed that a short spell at moderate heat killed them without ruining the taste. Applied to milk, it saved a great many children.
Probably not named after Caesar at all. Roman law required the operation on a dying mother — and Caesar's mother lived for decades after his birth. The likelier root is caedere, Latin for to cut.

Amelia Bloomer did not invent them — she promoted them in her newspaper, and the press attached her name. Women wearing them were mocked in the street, and the campaign was dropped as a distraction from the vote.

Named after a play. Sarah Bernhardt played Princess Fedora in 1882 wearing a soft centre-creased hat, and women adopted it as a symbol of the movement for women's rights before men took it over entirely.

John Stetson made a wide-brimmed hat on a prospecting trip to keep sun and rain off, and sold it off his own head for five dollars. He called the design the Boss of the Plains and built a factory on it.

Charles Macintosh spelled his name without the k. He glued two layers of cloth together with rubber dissolved in naphtha — a by-product of the gasworks — and made the first genuinely waterproof coat. The k crept in later.
Named for a battle, not a person. British troops at Balaclava in the Crimean winter of 1854 were sent knitted headgear from home because the army had not equipped them for the cold.

Louis Reard named his 1946 swimsuit after Bikini Atoll, where an atomic bomb had been tested four days earlier — he wanted a name that suggested an explosion. No Paris model would wear it, so he hired a dancer.

The fourth Earl of Chesterfield is said to have commissioned a sofa that would let a gentleman sit upright without creasing his suit. He is better remembered for letters of advice to his son that Samuel Johnson called immoral.

William Murphy was courting a singer while living in a one-room San Francisco apartment, and etiquette forbade a woman entering a bedroom. He designed a bed that folded into the wall, turning his bedroom into a parlour.

John Mason patented the screw-thread glass jar with a rubber-sealed lid in 1858, making home preserving safe and reliable. His patent expired, competitors flooded in, and he died poor while everyone else got rich.

Laszlo Biro was a journalist who noticed newspaper ink dried almost instantly while his fountain pen smudged. He built a pen that used the thicker ink with a rolling ball to feed it. Britain still calls every ballpoint a biro.

Earl Tupper's airtight seal sold badly in shops because nobody could see why it mattered. Brownie Wise worked out you had to demonstrate the burp in someone's living room, and invented the Tupperware party.

Candido Jacuzzi's young son had rheumatoid arthritis and needed hydrotherapy at hospital. The family made pumps for farms, so Candido built a portable pump to put the treatment in the family bath. The spa industry came later.

Damocles told the tyrant Dionysius how lucky he was, so Dionysius offered to swap places. Damocles enjoyed the throne until he looked up and saw a sword hanging over it by a single horsehair. He asked to leave.

Sisyphus cheated death twice — once by chaining up Death himself, so that for a while nobody on earth could die. His punishment was a boulder that always rolls back. Camus argued we must imagine him happy.

Tantalus stood in water that drained whenever he bent to drink, under fruit that swung away whenever he reached. English took his name for the very specific cruelty of something being just out of reach.
Narcissus saw his reflection in a pool, did not realise it was himself, and could not leave. The flower that grew where he died still bends its head toward water.

Oedipus was abandoned as a baby precisely so the prophecy could not come true, and it came true because he was abandoned. Freud borrowed the name in 1899 for a theory the play itself does not require.
It was a jar, not a box. Erasmus mistranslated the Greek pithos as pyxis in the sixteenth century and the mistake stuck. Pandora shut the lid with one thing still inside: hope.
Procrustes offered travellers a bed and guaranteed a perfect fit — by stretching anyone too short and cutting down anyone too tall. Theseus eventually gave him the same treatment on his own bed.

A teacher told that certain pupils are gifted will, without meaning to, treat them differently — and those pupils improve. Named after the sculptor who loved his statue into life, because expectation does the shaping.

Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold, and it did — including his food, his drink, and in some versions his daughter. He begged to have the gift taken back, and washed it off in a river.

When Odysseus sailed for Troy he left his son with a friend named Mentor. Athena kept borrowing that shape to deliver advice — so the word for a trusted guide is really the name of a goddess's disguise.
Ten years to sail home from a war that itself took ten years. Odysseus survives by lying, hiding and outthinking everything he meets, which makes him a strange sort of hero and a very durable one.

Twelve labours, each supposedly impossible: the lion, the hydra, the stables, the golden apples. He was given them as punishment, completed all twelve, and the word for an enormous task has been his ever since.
A lion at the front, a goat rising from the back, a snake for a tail. Even the Greeks found it absurd, which is why chimera came to mean a wild impossible idea rather than an actual monster.
Three heads, so one is always awake. The way past was music — Orpheus played him to sleep — or cake, since Romans buried honey cakes with their dead specifically as a bribe. Hence a sop to Cerberus.

Janus guarded doorways, with one face looking back and one forward. His temple doors in Rome stood open in wartime and shut in peace. In roughly seven hundred years they were recorded as closed only a handful of times.

Charles Goodyear spent years and several fortunes trying to make rubber stable, and found the answer by accidentally dropping a rubber-and-sulphur mixture on a hot stove. He named it for the Roman god of the forge, and died in debt.
The fastest-moving planet took the name of the fastest god. The liquid metal got it too, for rolling away the moment you touch it — and gave English mercurial for anyone whose mood does the same.
Everything military traces to Mars: martial arts, martial law, court-martial. March is his month too, because it was when the campaigning season opened and Roman armies could move again.

Medieval doctors believed the planet overhead at your birth set your temperament. Jupiter — Jove — produced the cheerful sort. Saturn produced the gloomy sort, which is why saturnine still means what it does.

skip_why: clinical/adult sense; excluded from kid-facing cards
story: From Venus, Roman goddess of love. A medical term with a mythological name, now largely replaced in clinical use by more precise language.

Pan was the goat-legged god of wild places, and travellers who heard an unexplained noise in an empty wood blamed him. That particular fear — sudden, irrational, contagious — is the one that kept his name.
Echo was a nymph who talked too much, and Hera cursed her to repeat only other people's last words. She fell in love with Narcissus and could never say so — only give him his own words back.
Iris was the rainbow, and the messenger who ran along it between gods and mortals. The coloured ring of your eye is named after her, and so is the flower, and so is the word iridescent.
Flora was the Roman goddess of flowers and spring, and her festival involved so much noise and colour that stricter Romans disapproved. Biologists took her name for all the plant life of a place.
Faunus was the Roman god of forests and wild animals, and his female counterpart Fauna gave her name to all animal life. Flora and fauna are a goddess and a goddess, still working as a pair.

skip_why: anatomical/adult sense; excluded from kid-facing cards
story: Hymen was the Greek god of weddings, invoked in marriage songs. The anatomical term borrowed his name much later.
Hymen was the Greek god of weddings, and a hymeneal is a wedding song. Greek marriage processions called his name aloud on the way to the bride's house, which is where the word comes from.
The Romans made him a chubby child with a bow. The Greeks knew him as Eros and took him rather more seriously — a primordial force older than most of the gods, not a decoration for a card.

Erebus was darkness itself, born near the beginning of things. A British polar ship took the name, and after it was lost in the Arctic, a volcano in Antarctica was named after the ship — darkness, twice removed.
Morpheus did not bring sleep; he supplied the people who appear in your dreams, taking their shapes himself. His name comes from morphe, the Greek for form.

A German pharmacist isolated it from opium in 1804 and named it after the god of dreams. He tested it on himself and on three boys, nearly killing all four, then spent much of his life addicted to it.

Hypnos was the Greek god of sleep, brother of Death and son of Night. Hypnosis is not really sleep at all — the name was chosen before anyone understood what was happening — and its coiner later regretted it.

Thanatos was the gentle personification of death, as distinct from the violent kind. Thanatology — the study of dying, grief and how people face the end — took his name rather than a harsher one deliberately.

From Hebe, goddess of youth, because the condition was first described in adolescents. Like several psychiatric terms built from Greek gods, it has largely been retired in favour of plainer clinical language.

Mnemosyne was memory, and the mother of all nine Muses — which makes memory, in Greek thinking, the parent of every art. Sensible, for a culture that recited Homer for centuries before writing it down.
A museum was originally a place belonging to the Muses — a shrine to the nine goddesses of the arts. The greatest of them, at Alexandria, was a research institute with the famous library attached.
Music means, literally, the art of the Muses. It covered poetry and dance as well as sound, because the Greeks did not separate them — a performance was all three at once.

Hygieia was the daughter of the god of medicine, and her job was keeping people well rather than curing them once sick. Her sister Panacea handled cures — and gave English a word for a remedy for everything.

Ancient physicians claimed descent from Asclepius, god of medicine, and called themselves Asclepiads. His snake-wound staff is still the symbol of medicine — though it is often confused with a different, two-snake staff belonging to Hermes.

The Roman spelling of Asclepius. When plague struck Rome in 293 BC the Senate sent for the god, and a snake from his temple reportedly boarded the ship and slid off onto an island in the Tiber, where they built him a temple.
In myth, the child of Hermes and Aphrodite was merged with a nymph into one body. The biological term is now generally reserved for plants and some animals rather than people.

Hermes Trismegistus was a legendary sage credited with secret writings. Alchemists working in that tradition developed a way of fusing glass to seal a vessel completely — so a hermetic seal is named after a wizard.

Atlas was condemned to hold up the sky forever. The top vertebra of your spine, which holds up your skull, carries his name — and the book of maps does too, from a picture of Atlas on the cover of an early collection.

His mother dipped him in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, holding him by the heel — the one spot the water never touched. The largest tendon in your body is named after the one weak point in a legend.
Caesar's name outlived his empire twice over: German emperors were Kaisers and Russian ones Tsars, both worn-down forms of the same word. Caesarian, meaning imperial, is the direct English adjective.
Renamed for Augustus in 8 BC. The story that he stole a day from February so his month would match Julius Caesar's is a medieval invention — but the Senate really did rename it for him.
Renamed for Julius Caesar after his death, in the month he was born. He had just reformed the calendar into something close to the one we use, so the honour was at least on topic.

An old medical term for nicotine poisoning, built from the name of the French diplomat who introduced tobacco to his queen as a headache cure. He would probably not have chosen this particular memorial.

Orwell wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four in 1948 and swapped the last two digits for the title. The word now gets used for any surveillance at all, which slightly misses the point — his real subject was the corruption of language.

Darwin sat on his theory for twenty years, worried about the reaction. He only published when a letter arrived from Alfred Russel Wallace describing the same idea — and their work was presented jointly.

Darwin never wrote survival of the fittest — Herbert Spencer coined it, and Darwin adopted it reluctantly in a later edition. Fittest means best-suited to the surroundings, not strongest, which is the misunderstanding that persists.

Gregor Mendel grew about 28,000 pea plants in a monastery garden and worked out the rules of inheritance. His paper was almost entirely ignored for thirty-four years, until three separate scientists rediscovered it at once.

Lamarck thought a giraffe that stretched for high leaves would pass longer necks to its young. He was wrong about the mechanism, but he was arguing that species change at all, decades before Darwin — which took some courage.

Pasteur's germ theory met fierce resistance from doctors who resented being told they carried disease on their hands. He was also a chemist, not a physician, which the medical establishment mentioned frequently.

Koch identified the bacteria behind anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera, and set out the rules for proving any such link. He and Pasteur were bitter rivals, and their national newspapers cheered them on.

Mendel's laws describe how traits pass on in neat ratios — but he chose pea characteristics that happened to be unusually simple. Most inheritance is far messier, which is partly why his results looked almost too tidy.

Linnaeus gave every living thing a two-word name, genus then species, replacing descriptions that ran to whole sentences. He also named himself: born Carl Nilsson, he took Linnaeus from a lime tree on the family farm.

Cuvier could reconstruct an entire animal from a few bones, and proved that species go extinct — an idea many found impossible, since it implied the creation was not perfect. He rejected evolution to his last day.
Buffon estimated the Earth was at least 75,000 years old by heating iron spheres and timing how long they took to cool. The Church objected. He apologised in print and went on believing it.

A Freudian slip is a mistake that supposedly reveals a hidden thought. Freud's own term was Fehlleistung — faulty achievement — and he collected examples obsessively, including a great many of his own.
Jung was Freud's chosen successor until they fell out permanently over how much of the mind is sexual. He went on to argue that certain images recur across all cultures, and called them archetypes.

Adler broke with Freud over the same question and built a psychology around the drive to overcome feelings of inferiority. He gave us inferiority complex, one of the few psychiatric terms everyone uses correctly.

Pavlov was studying digestion, not learning, and the dogs' drooling was ruining his measurements. He investigated the nuisance instead of eliminating it, and found conditioning. He was not, incidentally, ringing a bell — usually a metronome.

Skinner trained pigeons to guide missiles during the Second World War, and the system worked — the military just could not bring itself to trust it. He also raised his daughter's early months in a heated, filtered climate-controlled crib.

Piaget worked out his stages of child development largely by watching his own three children very closely and writing down everything. He published his first scientific paper, on an albino sparrow, at the age of eleven.

Maslow never drew his hierarchy as a pyramid — someone else added that later, and the shape implies a rigidity he did not intend. He was interested in what healthy people do, when psychology mostly studied illness.

Descartes is supposed to have thought of coordinates while lying in bed watching a fly on the ceiling and wondering how to describe its position with numbers. Every graph you have ever drawn descends from that fly.

Platonic love, in Plato, meant a love that climbs from a particular person toward beauty and truth themselves. English flattened it into love without romance, which Plato would have considered the least interesting part.

Aristotle tutored Alexander the Great, dissected sea creatures on Lesbos, and wrote the first surviving works on logic, physics and drama. For much of the Middle Ages, scholars simply called him The Philosopher.

Socrates wrote nothing. Everything we have comes from students, chiefly Plato. His method was to ask questions until the other person discovered their own answer had a hole in it — which made him popular with the young and not with anyone else.

Epicurus taught that the greatest pleasure is freedom from pain and anxiety, and lived on bread, water and the occasional pot of cheese. English turned his name into a word for a gourmet, which reverses him completely.
Named after a building. Zeno taught on a painted porch — a stoa — in Athens, and his followers were called the porch people. Their doctrine was that you control your judgements and nothing else.

From the Greek for dog-like. The Cynics lived rough on purpose, and Diogenes is supposed to have accepted the insult and adopted it. Modern cynicism — assuming bad motives — is a long way from the original.
A modern term for extreme self-neglect and hoarding. It is arguably misnamed: Diogenes chose poverty deliberately and owned almost nothing, which is close to the opposite of hoarding.
Euclid's Elements ran as a school textbook for over two thousand years — the longest run of any book but the Bible. Asked by a king for a shortcut, he replied that there is no royal road to geometry.

Pythagoras ran what was half a school and half a secret society, with rules against eating beans. The theorem was known to Babylonian mathematicians a thousand years earlier; his followers may have supplied the first proof.

Archimedes worked out how to measure the volume of a crown in the bath and, the story goes, ran into the street shouting. He was killed by a Roman soldier while drawing diagrams in the sand, reportedly telling him not to disturb them.

The bell curve turns up everywhere — heights, errors, exam marks — because adding up enough small independent effects produces it almost regardless of what those effects are. Gauss found it while analysing astronomical errors.

George Boole reduced logic to algebra with two values, true and false, in 1854. He thought he was studying the laws of thought. Ninety years later it turned out he had written the mathematics of every computer ever built.
An imaginary device with an infinite paper tape that reads, writes and moves one square at a time. Turing invented it to prove something impossible, and accidentally defined what a computer is.
